title: YOU CAN SPEAK IN TONGUES AND STILL HAVE A ROTTEN HEART: Why Paul Said “Fruit,” Not “Fruits” of the Spirit
paragraphs: YOU CAN SPEAK IN TONGUES AND STILL HAVE A ROTTEN HEART: Why Paul Said “Fruit,” Not “Fruits” of the Spirit

What if the greatest evidence that the Holy Spirit is transforming your life is not how loudly you worship, how much Scripture you memorize, or how powerfully you preach—but how you treat people when your flesh has every reason to do otherwise?
You prayed this morning.
You shared a Bible verse. You listened to worship music. You told someone that God is good. Perhaps you even encouraged someone who was struggling with their faith.
Then someone offended you.
Suddenly, the kindness disappeared. Your patience ran out. Your pride demanded recognition. Your mouth released words that your heart knew Jesus would never approve of.
And somewhere between your morning devotion and your evening anger, you became someone completely different from the Christian you claimed to be.
Does that sound painfully familiar?
Because sometimes the greatest contradiction in Christianity is not found in the unbeliever who refuses to enter a church.
It is found in the believer who knows how to look spiritual without allowing the Holy Spirit to transform the deepest parts of their character.
We know how to raise our hands in worship, but struggle to lower our pride in an argument.
We know how to ask God for forgiveness, but refuse to forgive someone who wounded us.
We preach grace to strangers while withholding it from our own families.
We want the power of the Holy Spirit without surrendering to the transforming work of the Holy Spirit.
And perhaps this is why one seemingly small grammatical detail in Paul's letter to the Galatians deserves far more attention than we have given it.
Galatians 5:22–23 declares:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, meekness, temperance: against such there is no law.” — KJV
Read that again.
Paul did not say the fruits of the Spirit.
He said the fruit of the Spirit.
Singular.
In the original Koine Greek, the passage reads:
Ὁ δὲ καρπὸς τοῦ πνεύματός ἐστιν ἀγάπη, χαρά, εἰρήνη, μακροθυμία, χρηστότης, ἀγαθωσύνη, πίστις, πραΰτης, ἐγκράτεια· κατὰ τῶν τοιούτων οὐκ ἔστιν νόμος.
Transliterated:
Ho de karpos tou pneumatos estin agapē, chara, eirēnē, makrothymia, chrēstotēs, agathōsynē, pistis, prautēs, enkrateia; kata tōn toioutōn ouk estin nomos.
A faithful English rendering is:
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.”
The Greek word καρπός (karpos) is a singular noun meaning fruit, produce, yield, or the result of something.
Its plural form is καρποί (karpoi).
Paul uses the singular.
Now notice something even more fascinating.
Just three verses earlier, in Galatians 5:19, Paul writes:
Φανερὰ δέ ἐστιν τὰ ἔργα τῆς σαρκός.
Phanera de estin ta erga tēs sarkos.
“Now the works of the flesh are evident.”
The word ἔργα (erga) is plural, meaning works or deeds.
The works of the flesh.
The fruit of the Spirit.

The grammatical contrast is real. Although the singular noun karpos can function collectively and does not, by itself, prove that all nine qualities are inseparable or develop equally, Paul's wider teaching presents them together as the result of a life being shaped by the same Holy Spirit.
These are not nine unrelated spiritual achievements.
They are interconnected expressions of the Spirit's transforming work.
And that changes how we should understand Christian maturity.
You cannot treat the fruit of the Spirit like a spiritual buffet.
“I'll take joy, but I don't want patience.”
“I like peace, but forgiveness is asking too much.”
“I want goodness, but gentleness makes me look weak.”
“I love Jesus, but don't expect me to control my temper.”
We laugh because it sounds ridiculous.
But how many of us are living exactly like that?
How many Christians have mistaken their natural personality for spiritual maturity?
A naturally quiet person may appear peaceful while secretly harboring bitterness.
A cheerful person may appear joyful while depending entirely on favorable circumstances.
A generous person may perform good deeds while craving recognition.
A disciplined person may exercise self-control while being merciless toward those who struggle.
Outward resemblance does not automatically establish inward transformation.
The fruit Paul describes is not merely a collection of admirable personality traits. It is the character that the Holy Spirit cultivates in those who belong to Christ.
And the difference becomes painfully visible when life stops cooperating with us.
Love is tested when someone becomes difficult to love.
Joy is tested when circumstances give us reasons to despair.
Peace is tested when the future becomes uncertain.
Patience is tested when God does not answer according to our timetable.
Kindness is tested when someone treats us unfairly.
Goodness is tested when compromise would benefit us.
Faithfulness is tested when obedience becomes costly.
Gentleness is tested when we have the power to retaliate.
Self-control is tested when nobody is watching.
The fruit of the Spirit is often most clearly revealed when the flesh has the strongest opportunity to take control.
Imagine a woman sitting alone in her bedroom after discovering that someone she trusted had betrayed her.
Her phone is in her hand.
She has already typed the message.
Every accusation. Every insult. Every painful detail she could expose publicly.
She knows exactly how to destroy the reputation of the person who destroyed her peace.
Her finger hovers over the screen.
Then something within her brings the words of Jesus to remembrance.
“But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you…” — Matthew 5:44, KJV
She begins to cry.
Not because the betrayal suddenly stops hurting.
Not because the other person deserves her forgiveness.
Not because what happened was acceptable.
But because she realizes that another person's sin does not have to become the master of her own character.
She deletes the message.
She may still establish boundaries. She may still seek justice. She may still need counseling, protection, and time to heal.
Forgiveness does not require returning to an abusive situation or pretending that wrongdoing never happened.
But in that moment, she refuses to let revenge become her ruler.
That is what spiritual fruit can look like.
No microphone.
No stage.
No applause.
Just a wounded human being surrendering a painful moment to Jesus Christ.
And heaven sees what social media never will.
Perhaps you are that person.
Perhaps your greatest spiritual battle is not happening inside a church but inside your marriage, your workplace, your private conversations, your thoughts, or the silence of your bedroom.
Perhaps you are fighting an anger nobody understands.
Perhaps you are exhausted from forgiving people who never apologized.
Perhaps you have been praying for years, wondering why you still struggle with the same weaknesses.
Before you condemn yourself, understand this:
Fruit grows.
It does not become mature overnight.
A seed does not become a fully developed tree simply because someone commands it to grow faster.
There are seasons of rooting, pruning, nourishment, waiting, and development.
Jesus Himself used this imagery in John 15:4–5:
“Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me.”
And then He said:
“I am the vine, ye are the branches…”
The Greek verb translated as “abide” is μένω (menō), meaning to remain, stay, or continue.
Jesus was not teaching His disciples to manufacture spiritual fruit independently of Him.
He was teaching them to remain in Him.
The branch does not produce fruit by separating itself from the vine and trying harder.
Its life depends upon its connection to the vine.
Likewise, Christian transformation is not accomplished through religious performance detached from Christ.
We cannot manufacture holiness through appearances.
We cannot pretend our way into spiritual maturity.
We cannot heal the corruption of the human heart through public reputation.
We need Jesus.
And this brings us to the beautiful depth of the nine qualities Paul identifies.
The first is ἀγάπη (agapē), love.
In this context, it is not merely romantic affection or emotional attachment. It is love expressed through seeking another person's good, patterned after the self-giving love of Christ.
Romans 5:8 reminds us that Christ died for us while we were still sinners.
Jesus did not wait until we became worthy of His love.
His love reached us in our rebellion.
That is why Christian love cannot be reduced to loving only those who make us comfortable.
Then comes χαρά (chara), joy.
Biblical joy is not the denial of sorrow. It is gladness rooted in God that can coexist with suffering.
Paul describes believers as “sorrowful, yet alway rejoicing” in 2 Corinthians 6:10.
You can cry and still possess joy.
You can grieve and still trust God.
You can walk through a season of depression or emotional exhaustion without your suffering automatically proving an absence of the Holy Spirit.
Joy is not a requirement to wear a fake smile.
It is the hope that darkness does not have the final word.
Then there is εἰρήνη (eirēnē), peace.
This word carries the sense of peace, harmony, and well-being. In the Christian life, it is deeply connected to our reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ, as Romans 5:1 teaches.
Peace is not always the absence of conflict.
Sometimes it is the presence of trust while conflict surrounds you.
You may not understand what God is doing, but you are learning that uncertainty does not mean abandonment.
Then Paul names μακροθυμία (makrothymia), patience or longsuffering.
It describes patience, forbearance, and restraint, particularly when dealing with provocation or difficult circumstances.
Think about how patient God has been with you.
How many times did you promise Him that you would change?
How many times did you return to the very thing you said you had surrendered?
How many opportunities did He give you to repent?
Romans 2:4 teaches that God's kindness is intended to lead us toward repentance.
When we remember the patience God has extended toward us, we begin to understand why patience toward others matters.
Next is χρηστότης (chrēstotēs), kindness.
Kindness is goodness expressed through a gracious disposition toward others.
It is how you speak to someone who cannot benefit you.
It is how you treat the exhausted employee who made a mistake.
It is how you respond to the struggling believer who confesses something embarrassing.
Kindness does not abandon truth.
It refuses to use truth as an excuse for cruelty.
Then comes ἀγαθωσύνη (agathōsynē), goodness.
This refers to moral goodness and uprightness expressed through character and action.
Goodness is choosing what honors God even when dishonesty would be easier, more profitable, or more popular.
It is integrity when there is no audience.
It is doing what is right when doing what is wrong would never be discovered by another human being.
Then Paul writes πίστις (pistis).

This Greek word can mean faith, trust, or faithfulness, depending on its context. Many modern translations render it as “faithfulness” in Galatians 5:22, emphasizing reliability and fidelity as qualities of Spirit-shaped character.
Faithfulness is not merely enthusiasm when Christianity feels exciting.
It is continuing to follow Jesus when obedience is inconvenient.
When the prayers seem unanswered.
When the emotions disappear.
When the crowd walks away.
When nobody celebrates your sacrifice.
Then comes πραΰτης (prautēs), gentleness or meekness.
Gentleness is not cowardice.
Jesus described Himself as gentle and humble in heart in Matthew 11:29, yet He never lacked courage or authority.
Gentleness is strength exercised without unnecessary harshness.
It is the ability to correct without humiliating.
To disagree without dehumanizing.
To defend truth without becoming consumed by hatred.
Finally, Paul names ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia), self-control.
It refers to restraint or mastery over one's desires and impulses.
It is saying no when temptation promises temporary pleasure.
It is refusing to let anger control your mouth, lust control your decisions, greed control your priorities, or pride control your relationships.
It is not the absence of temptation.
It is learning, through the Spirit's help, not to obey every desire that demands your surrender.
Nine qualities.
One fruit.
One divine source.
Different expressions of a life being transformed through Jesus Christ.
Notice how beautifully these qualities work together.
Love without self-control can become indulgence.
Truthfulness without gentleness can become unnecessarily harsh.
Patience without moral goodness can become tolerance of wrongdoing.
Joy without love can become self-centered pleasure.
Faithfulness without kindness can become rigid and unmerciful.
The Spirit's work is not about developing one impressive quality while deliberately protecting the sinful areas we refuse to surrender.
He is transforming the whole person.
And perhaps that is what makes this passage so uncomfortable.
Because we would rather be admired for our strongest spiritual qualities than confronted about our weakest ones.
We want people to notice our generosity without questioning our pride.
Our biblical knowledge without confronting our arrogance.
Our ministry without examining our marriage.
Our public testimony without investigating our private character.
But Jesus is not interested in merely improving the image we present to the world.
He came to redeem the person hiding behind it.
This is also why spiritual gifts and spiritual fruit must not be confused.
In 1 Corinthians 12, Paul explains that the Holy Spirit distributes different gifts to different believers according to His will.
But in 1 Corinthians 13:1–3, immediately after discussing spiritual gifts, Paul delivers a devastating warning.
A person may speak with extraordinary tongues, possess remarkable knowledge, demonstrate great faith, or make tremendous sacrifices, yet without love, those accomplishments amount to nothing.
Think about that.
You can impress an audience without loving the people closest to you.
You can possess theological knowledge without practicing humility.
You can build a religious platform while neglecting your own spiritual condition.
You can become famous for talking about Jesus while resisting the character of Jesus.
Spiritual gifts are not substitutes for spiritual fruit.
And the size of someone's ministry is not an infallible measurement of their maturity.
God is not merely concerned with what He can accomplish through you. He is also concerned with what He is transforming within you.
Be honest before God.
Which quality of the fruit of the Spirit is most difficult for you right now?
Is it patience?
Gentleness?
Self-control?
Love toward someone who wounded you?
Not as a religious performance. Not because commenting earns God's favor. But as an honest acknowledgment that you are still growing and that you need His grace.
Someone else reading your response may discover that they are not the only Christian fighting a difficult spiritual battle.
We need more believers who are willing to admit that they are being transformed rather than pretending they have already arrived.
Because the Gospel is not the story of perfect people proving their righteousness to God.
It is the story of a perfect Savior redeeming sinners who could never save themselves.
Galatians 5:24 continues:
“And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts.”
Then verse 25 declares:
“If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit.”
The Greek word translated as “walk” in verse 25 is στοιχέω (stoicheō), which carries the sense of walking in line with, keeping in step with, or following an established direction.
Paul is calling believers to live consistently with the new life they have received through the Spirit.
This involves daily surrender.
Daily repentance.
Daily obedience.
Daily dependence upon Christ.
Not because these things purchase salvation, but because salvation changes the direction of our lives.
Ephesians 2:8–10 establishes the order beautifully: we are saved by grace through faith, not by works, and we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The works are not the price of salvation.
They are its intended result.
The fruit is not the root of our salvation.
Jesus Christ is the source of our new life.
Never reverse that order.
Otherwise, you will spend your entire Christian life trying to produce enough goodness to convince God to love you.
But the Gospel announces something infinitely greater.
Christ came for sinners.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He died and rose again.
Through Him, forgiveness, reconciliation, and new life are offered to those who repent and believe.
And the Holy Spirit works within believers, transforming them into the likeness of Christ, as 2 Corinthians 3:18 teaches.
You may have a scandalous past.
You may have broken promises.
You may have destroyed relationships through anger, selfishness, addiction, dishonesty, or pride.
You may have spent years becoming someone you never intended to become.
But your past does not place you beyond the redeeming power of Jesus Christ.
Grace does not pretend your sin never happened.
Grace confronts your sin, offers forgiveness through Christ, and calls you into a different life.
The same Jesus who forgives your past also calls you to surrender your present.
And sometimes the evidence of His transforming grace will not be a dramatic testimony delivered before thousands of people.
Sometimes it will be the apology you finally offer your spouse.
The bitterness you begin to release.
The temptation you refuse.
The truth you confess.
The angry response you choose not to send.
The kindness you extend to someone who cannot repay you.
The prayer you whisper after failing again.
These moments may appear insignificant to the world.
But they are part of the ordinary, often unseen process of spiritual growth.
Do not confuse slow growth with hopelessness.
Do not use grace as an excuse to remain unchanged, either.
Repent when you fall.
Seek accountability when you struggle.
Remain in Scripture.
Pray honestly.
Walk alongside mature believers.
Depend upon the Holy Spirit.
Keep returning to Jesus.
And when you see spiritual fruit developing in your life, remember who deserves the glory.
Not your religious reputation.
Not your willpower alone.
Not your ability to appear righteous.
Jesus Christ.
There may come a day when anger, temptation, discouragement, or bitterness makes you forget everything you have just read.
Return to these Scriptures when that day comes.
Your willingness to share biblical truth may help someone rediscover the hope of the Gospel.
We want this community to be a place where Scripture confronts sin without abandoning the sinner, where truth and grace meet, and where broken people are continually pointed toward Jesus Christ.
Ministry requires time, labor, resources, and the faithful generosity of people who believe in its mission.

Galatians 6:6 encourages those who receive instruction in the Word to share good things with those who teach. Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come willingly from the heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
It is an opportunity to participate in a mission that seeks to glorify Christ by making biblical truth, encouragement, and discipleship resources accessible to more people.
If God has used this ministry to encourage you, and you have the means to support it, we warmly invite you to become part of its continuing mission.
Jesus Christ is not for sale.
Before you leave, remember the seemingly small word that started this entire conversation.
Fruit.
Not a collection of religious trophies.
Not a competition between Christians.
Not a carefully constructed image of perfection.
The fruit of the Spirit.
The beautiful evidence of the Holy Spirit working within ordinary, imperfect, redeemed human beings who are learning to surrender their lives to an extraordinary Savior.
Perhaps you are not yet as patient as you should be.
Perhaps your love still struggles against bitterness.
Perhaps your peace is fragile, your gentleness inconsistent, and your self-control still developing.
Bring all of it to Jesus.
The parts you celebrate.
The parts you conceal.
The parts you are ashamed to admit.
The parts you thought would never change.
He already knows.
And still, He calls you to repentance, faith, obedience, and abiding in Him.
The Christian life is not about convincing the world that you have never been broken.
It is about allowing the world to witness what the grace of Jesus Christ can do with a broken person who has surrendered to Him.
One day, your greatest testimony may not be the scandal Jesus rescued you from, but the person you no longer become when life gives you every reason to return to it.
